Moira Deeming currently has top spot on the Liberal Party's Western Metropolitan ticket. (AAP: James Ross)

The Liberal Party has agreed to call off a meeting to decide whether Moira Deeming would retain her preselection for the upcoming election, after the MP launched legal action to prevent it.

The party's state executive was to meet on Friday evening, after Mrs Deeming refused to apologise to former leader Matthew Guy, over her allegations he put her in a headlock at a community event.

The dispute will return to court later this month.

Victorian MP Moira Deeming has won a two-week reprieve as a Liberal candidate for the November state election, after the party agreed in the Supreme Court to cancel imminent plans to revoke her preselection.

Mrs Deeming sought an injunction against the party and president Brian Loughnane to stop the state executive from disendorsing her candidacy, after she refused to apologise to her party room colleague Matthew Guy.

She had accused Mr Guy of putting her in a headlock at a Macedonian community event in May.

The upper house MP first took her complaint to the state opposition leader's office before reporting the allegation to Victoria Police.

Victoria Police dismissed the complaint after reviewing CCTV footage, which appeared to show Mr Guy place his hand on Mrs Deeming's back during a conversation at the crowded Sunshine venue.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson joined Mr Guy's demands for an apology, but Mrs Deeming refused.

The Liberal Party's state executive was due to meet at 6.30pm on Friday to revoke her preselection for the Western Metropolitan Region in the upper house, a position that would have guaranteed her election in November.

Mrs Deeming was offered the opportunity to argue her case before the state executive vote.

But she launched the last-ditch Supreme Court action late on Thursday in an attempt to save her political career.

The Liberal Party on Friday afternoon agreed not to remove her as the candidate until the dispute can be heard later this month.

The Liberal Party were expecting the legal challenge and were confident of their legal position.

Three-quarters of the 18-person executive would need to agree to disendorse Mrs Deeming.

Members told the ABC they were hopeful of a unanimous outcome against her.

The executive is not seeking to kick Mrs Deeming out of the Liberal Party as a rank-and-file member, or the parliamentary party room.

CCTV footage showed Matthew Guy placing a hand on Moira Deeming's back. (Supplied)

Ms Wilson did not address the media on Friday, but on Thursday said she would not allow distractions as the Coalition seeks to topple Labor at the November election.

Mrs Deeming on Monday released a statement through her lawyer, conceding she had misunderstood the meaning of the term “headlock” but had made the complaint in good faith.

One Nation federal leader Pauline Hanson ruled out drafting Mrs Deeming as a candidate for making the allegation and failing to apologise.

"No. I don't want her. No, no," Senator Hanson told 3AW on Thursday.
